```{r setup}
library(knapsack)
suppressWarnings(RNGversion(min(as.character(getRversion()), "3.5.3")))
set.seed(42, kind = "Mersenne-Twister", normal.kind = "Inversion")
n <- 2000
knapsack_objects <- data.frame(w = sample(1:4000, size = n, replace = TRUE),
                               v = runif(n = n, 0, 10000))
```

## Brute force search

```{r}
brute_force_knapsack(x = knapsack_objects[1:8, ], W = 3500)
```

**Question:** How much time does it take to run the algorithm for n = 16 objects?

```{r}
system.time(brute_force_knapsack(x = knapsack_objects[1:16, ], W = 3500))
```

Answer: about X seconds. The time doubles for every extra object, since there are 2^n combinations.

## Dynamic programming

```{r}
knapsack_dynamic(x = knapsack_objects[1:8, ], W = 3500)
system.time(knapsack_dynamic(x = knapsack_objects[1:500, ], W = 3500))
```

Answer: about X seconds for n = 500. Time grows as O(W n).

## Greedy heuristic

```{r}
greedy_knapsack(x = knapsack_objects[1:800, ], W = 3500)
set.seed(42)
big <- data.frame(w = sample(1:4000, size = 1e6, replace = TRUE),
                  v = runif(n = 1e6, 0, 10000))
system.time(greedy_knapsack(x = big, W = 3500))
```

Answer: about X seconds for n = 1 000 000. Dominated by the sort, O(n log n).

## Profiling and optimization

Using `profvis`, the bottleneck in `knapsack_dynamic()` was the double `for` loop
over items and capacities. Replacing the inner loop with a vectorized `pmax()`
over all capacities reduced the time for n = 500 from about X s to about Y s
(roughly Z times faster). In the greedy function, using `cumsum()` instead of a
loop that adds items one by one avoids growing a vector inside a loop.
